translation:
# CAPVT III.

Observe, furthermore, the conditions of a true and candid friend at a wedding.

First, he says, *He stands*, which is to say, he is prepared to serve the bridegroom. For it is the place of servants to stand; it is the place of masters to sit. The bridegroom ought to sit with the bride, while good friends stand by, prepared for service.

Next, *he hears him*, which is to say, he is obedient to his word. Neither the voice nor the command of any other prevails here; only the bridegroom commands with the authority of ordering, such that it is a crime not to listen to him. He alone is heard because he alone is obeyed.

Thirdly, *he rejoices with joy*; that is, the true friend has nothing sweeter than to see the bridegroom glorified with the bride.

Finally, *he rejoices because of the voice of the bridegroom*, which is to say, he does not serve his own advantage or his own honors, but rather the voice of the bridegroom. John attributes these virtues to himself as a friend of Christ. I am prepared (he says) to serve; hence, standing, I stand. Next, I hear his voice alone, not yours, and even less that of others. Thirdly, I rejoice with him, not with you. I would rather have you suffer, so that I may rejoice with Christ and his bride. Finally, I have no other cause for joy than the voice of Christ, the true bridegroom. Wherefore, be gone with your envy and <term>φιλονεικία</term> <gloss>spirit of contention</gloss>. Rather, strive to bring the bride to Christ.

The nature of monarchy is one thing, that of aristocracy another, that of democracy another, which, if they are mixed, extinguish each other: and different laws also befit monarchical administration, others aristocratic, others democratic, because they are different modes of administration. Hence also there arises an incurable error in the republic among those who promise that they will reform everything, because they confuse these things, as if on a stage they wish to arrange all things with one boot and one rule, when yet one shoe does not fit every foot, or one foot does not have every shoe that fits it.

4 From this it also follows that all most corrupt things follow, and the people and the republic are necessarily agitated by seditions and swords. Unless each of the three received species of a republic is preserved in its own nature, it is necessary—and it happens easily—that they collapse into their neighboring vices: monarchy has a neighboring vice, tyranny, into which it declines with little effort.

The government of the best men, or aristocracy, easily declines also into an allied vice, namely the power of the few, with the other best men expelled, just as democracy, or the authority of the whole people, declines into plebeian madness and lawless liberty. See Aristotle in the third book of the *Politics*, chapter five, and the fourth book, chapter two.

<margin>a In the epitome of his book 6.</margin> It has been observed by Polybius, most excellently, that just as rust to iron and worms or wood-borers to wood, when they mix, bring ruin, so that even if they escape all external harms, they are consumed by those things which are innate to them: in this way also to republics, for every one according to its nature, a certain peculiar malice grows and adheres. As for example a kingdom, which is monarchy among the willing, becomes tyranny; aristocracy becomes oligarchy; democracy becomes bestial, a *chaerocracy* <gloss>mob-rule</gloss> or sedition of the plebeians.

<margin>b Diogenes Laertius in the life of Plato, book 3.</margin> Plato, distributing the city or polity into five species, has encompassed the legitimate and the illegitimate or deficient republics. He says there are popular, aristocratic, oligarchic, royal, and tyrannical republics. Popular, in those cities in which the matter is acted upon according to the command of the multitude and magistrates are chosen by its nod, and laws are passed according to its judgment.

Aristocracy, or the rule of the best, where neither the rich nor the poor, nor those illustrious by nobility or glory, dominate, but those alone who are the best in the city administer the matter.

Oligarchy, when magistrates are chosen by property qualifications, for they are fewer than the poor.

5 He says a kingdom is twofold: one according to law, another according to lineage. He says the kingdom of the Carthaginians consists according to law, since it is civil; but that of the Lacedaemonians according to lineage, for they have a certain succession through lineage; but it is called a tyranny when citizens, impelled and forced by violence, are ruled by someone.

Sic erit vana differentia, quā Plinius herbam ab arbore distingui vult. Ad Hellenii locum lib. 7. cap. de portulaca respondetur, non peccant contra librorum fidem qui adrachnen scribunt. In Veneta antiquissima editione constanter adrachne scribitur, nisi quod lib. 16. cap. 22. legatur, inter utraque genera sunt andrachne, pro quo in vulgata editione adrachne. Quomodo etiam locis citatis in antiquissima Parmensi legitur. Apud Graecos auctores fatendum, passim legi *ἀνδράχλην*, si unum locum exceperis Theophrasti lib. 1. hist. cap. 8. ubi in Lugd. editione *ἀδράχνη* legitur. Sed Plinii loco citato, mendosa & corrupta reliqua Theoph. loca, ubi *ἀνδράχλη* legitur, doctissimi afferunt. Quod autem scribit doctiss. vir, nullam diversitatem litteræ esse inter adrachnen & andrachnen, verū in altera dictione litteram esse minus; id fatendum est, si strictè verba Plinii sumantur; sin verò paulò laxius accipiamus, secus res sese habet. Nam ubi littera deest, ibi & litteræ est diversitas: nempe quod una absit quę in altera adest. Atque ea Plinii mens, si antiqua & Veneta & Parmenfis lectio vera. Sed in tanta rerum diversitate, & obscuritate quilibet sua fruatur opinione licet. Cæterùm, quod etiam pro altera facit opinione, hodie non *ἀδράχλη* à Græcis sed *ἀδραχλα* vocatur, ut refert ex Honorii Belli epistolis Carolus Clufius.

*Μεγέθει δ’ οὐκ ἄγαν μέγα.* Hoc de folio Plinius. Cæterùm, inquit, adrachne est sylvestris arbor, neque in planis nascens, simili unedoni, folio tantùm minore & nunquam decidente. Quod de arbore Græcus, id de folio Latinus. Falsum est, folia adrachnes minora esse quam arbuti; majora & latiora sunt.

*Tὸν δὲ φλοιὸν λευκόν* &c. Æstivo tempore quando rumpitur cortex, colore est medio inter pallidum, & cineraceum: sed hoc non potuit novisse Theoph. Saltem non scripsit *λευκόν*, verùm *λεῖον*. Quod de myrrha accepit Plinius, corticem levem, inquit, similemque unedoni, *Ἀδράχλην* quandoque interpretatur unedonem, quod adrachne unedoni satis similis sit, & in Latio cœlo magis cognita unedo quam adrachne, quæ arbor est Græco ac Cretenfi folo familiaris. Nomen habet apud Latinos. Ideò unedonem pro adrachne substituit. Falluntur enim qui *ἀδράχλην* arborem reddunt portulacam. Hoc obiter. Nam cortex rumpitur & finditur gelu. Et hæc causa est *ῥηξιφλοίας* in multis arboribus. Ita multis placet viris etiam doctissimis. Aliter tamen res se habet. To the passage of Helladius in book 7, chapter on purslane, it is responded that they do not sin against the fidelity of the books who write *adrachnen*. In the most ancient Venetian edition, it is constantly written *adrachne*, except that in book 16, chapter 22, it is read: *among both kinds are the andrachne*, for which in the vulgate edition [it is] *adrachne*. Just as also in the places cited it is read in the most ancient Parmese [edition]. Among Greek authors it must be admitted that <term>ἀνδράχλην</term> is read everywhere, if you except one place in Theophrastus, *History of Plants* book 1, chapter 8, where in the Lyon edition <term>ἀδράχνη</term> is read. But in the cited passage of Pliny, the most learned men adduce that the other places in Theophrastus, where <term>ἀνδράχλη</term> is read, are faulty and corrupted. But what the most learned man writes, that there is no diversity of a letter between *adrachnen* and *andrachnen*, but that there is one letter less in the other word; that must be admitted if the words of Pliny are taken strictly; but if we take them a little more loosely, the matter is otherwise. For where a letter is missing, there also is the diversity of a letter: namely, that one is absent which is present in the other. And that is the mind of Pliny, if the ancient and Venetian and Parmese reading is true. But in such a diversity and obscurity of things, let everyone enjoy their own opinion. Moreover, what also makes for the other opinion, today it is called not <term>ἀδράχλη</term> by the Greeks but <term>ἀδραχλα</term>, as Carolus Clusius reports from the letters of Honorius Bellus. *Μεγέθει δ’ οὐκ ἄγαν μέγα* <gloss>In size not very large</gloss>. Pliny [says] this concerning the leaf. Moreover, he says, the *adrachne* is a wild tree, not growing in plains, similar to the *unedo*, with a leaf only smaller and never falling. Yet the matter is otherwise. The bark is not ruptured in winter, but in summer; the bark in winter is smooth, by no means ruptured. Therefore I keep the vulgate reading, and I read: <term>Φλοιὸν λευκὸν περιαπορηγνύμενον</term>; because the bark when it is ruptured in summer is in color between white and ash-colored, which deserves to be called white. But it matters not whether you read <term>λευκόν</term> or <term>λεῖον</term>, if you say <term>λευκόν</term> when the bark is ruptured and falls, as he writes in book 1, chapter 8. Clusius and Alpinus describe the Adrachne; and indeed Clusius in chapter 31, book 1 of his *History*, in these words: *Purslane,* he says (Honorius Bellus, Cretan Physician), *or the* <term>ἀδράχλη</term> *of Theophrastus, grows frequently in Crete, in the White Mountains, and elsewhere among the rocks, in the manner of a shrub rather than a tree; it is evergreen, and has leaves so similar to laurel [leaves] that they are distinguished only by smell. (Theophrastus observed all these things.) It brings forth flower and fruit twice, like the arbutus, and indeed [it brings forth] this [fruit] so similar that you could in no way distinguish one from the other. Carolus Clusius in book 1 of *Rariorum Plantarum* expressed the icon from Honorius Bellus, having also fruits similar to the arbutus. And if a pledge was given to Saturninus, which is said by you very often, it was not C. Rabirius, but C. Marius who gave it; and he also violated it, if he did not stand by the pledge. How, Labienus, could that pledge be given without a decree of the senate? Are you so much a stranger to this city, so ignorant of our discipline and custom, that you do not know these things? That you seem to be traveling in a foreign state, not to be holding a magistracy in your own? What, he says, can these things now harm C. Marius, since he lacks sense and life? Is it truly so? Would C. Marius have lived through such great labors and dangers if he had thought nothing further of himself and his glory than what the limits of life demanded? But, I believe, when he had routed innumerable forces of the enemy in Italy and freed the Republic from siege, he thought that all his deeds would die with him. It is not so, citizens; nor does any one of us engage in the dangers of the Republic with praise and virtue without being led by the hope of posterity and its fruit. Therefore, while for many other reasons the minds of good men seem to me to be divine and eternal, they seem so especially because the soul of every excellent and most wise man perceives the future so that it appears to look at nothing but what is everlasting. Wherefore, I for my part attest to the minds of C. Marius and the other most wise and brave citizens, which seem to me to have departed from the life of men to the religion and sanctity of the gods, that I think it must be fought for their fame, glory, and memory no differently than for the shrines and temples of our fathers; and if I had to take up arms for their praise, I would take them up no less vigorously than they took them up for our common safety. For indeed, citizens, nature has circumscribed a small course of life for us, but an immense one of glory. Therefore, if we honor those who have already departed from life, we will leave a more just condition of death for ourselves. But if you, Labienus, neglect those whom we can no longer see, do you think it is not necessary to consider even those whom you do see?
